spec.full_target:
Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
spec.conclusion: dim_H(F)=D+1, where F=E×[0,1] has the Euclidean product metric and D=dim_H(E); equivalently dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1 in ℝ^{n+1}.

definitions.type: family of Euclidean metric spaces indexed by natural numbers, together with their coordinate notation
definitions.definition: For each natural k, V(k)=ℝ^k, the functions from {0,...,k-1} to ℝ, with distance d(x,y)=(Σ_{j=0}^{k-1}(x_j-y_j)^2)^(1/2) and its metric topology and Borel measurable structure. V(0) consists of the single empty tuple. ℝ has its usual absolute-value distance. V(k)×ℝ always means the metric with squared distance d(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2, not the max-product metric. Concatenation (x,t)↦(x_0,...,x_{k-1},t) specifies the identification with V(k+1).

definitions.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric or extended metric space
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space X and A⊆X, diam(A)=sup{edist(x,y):x∈A,y∈A} in [0,∞], with supremum of the empty set equal to 0. On a metric space edist is ordinary distance viewed in [0,∞]. This is the native Metric.ediam. When diam(A) is bounded by a finite scale we identify it with its finite nonnegative real value. In particular empty sets and singletons have diameter zero.

definitions.type: positive-exponent unnormalized Hausdorff contents and measure, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This

binders.type: countable family of subsets of that Euclidean space

definitions.type: native Hausdorff measures on Borel extended metric spaces, indexed by real exponents
definitions.definition: μH[d] on a Borel extended metric space X denotes MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure d, defined natively as Measure.mkMetric(r↦r^d), the metric outer-measure construction with diameter gauge r^d followed by its Borel measure. The metric outer construction is the supremum over positive extended scales r of the infimum of Σ_i (sup_{h:U_i≠∅} diam(U_i)^d) over sequences U:ℕ→Set X covering the set and satisfying diam(U_i)≤r. Empty summands are zero, including at exponent zero. Native ENNReal real powers are used. The value formula for the resulting measure on arbitrary subsets is established by the registered native theorem; its identification with H for positive exponents is proved below.

binders.type: extended metric space with its Borel measurable structure

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of a subset of a metric space, valued in [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For a subset A of a metric space with its Borel structure, dim_H(A)=sup{u:u∈[0,∞) is finite and μH[u](A)=∞}, with supremum of the empty set zero. The metric space may be borelized when no measurable structure was specified. This is the native dimH definition. Thus dim_H(∅)=0 by this convention. In this task it is applied to Euclidean subsets and the Euclidean product metric of V(n)×ℝ.

definitions.type: subset of V(n)×ℝ with the Euclidean product metric
definitions.definition: F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E,t∈I}, using the squared-distance product metric specified in V. Its Euclidean identification is the concatenation map to V(n+1).
D=dim_H(E). When finiteness is proved, finite dimensions are also viewed as nonnegative real numbers through the canonical inclusion ℝ≥0→[0,∞].

definitions.type: predicate on subsets of metric spaces
definitions.definition: Compact(A) means that every family of open sets whose union contains A has a finite subfamily whose union contains A. The word compact has this finite-open-subcover meaning throughout.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on the Borel real line, also evaluated as outer measure on arbitrary sets
definitions.definition: λ is the native MeasureTheory.volume on ℝ, equivalently the Lebesgue measure whose outer measure is the infimum of sums of lengths of countable open-interval covers. As for any measure, λ is monotone, has λ(∅)=0, and is countably additive on disjoint measurable sets. These measure axioms are part of the measure structure, not any assertion of measurability of the arbitrary covering sets in this proof.

definitions.type: nonnegative Lebesgue integral for an arbitrary measure on a measurable space
definitions.definition: For a measurable space X, a measure ν on it, and f:X→[0,∞], LInt(ν,f)=∫⁻ f dν is the supremum of the simple-function integrals Σ_a a ν(g^{-1}{a}) over nonnegative measurable finite-range simple functions g≤f, with 0·∞=0. This is the native MeasureTheory.lintegral. For measurable f the value may be ∞; no finite-integrability premise is implicit.

locals.type: Euclidean space with its Borel measurable structure
locals.declaration: Let X be any Euclidean space, including dimension zero, with its Borel measurable structure.
Fix an arbitrary real s; positivity is assumed only in the corresponding local implications.
For the monotonicity assertion fix B⊆X and assume A⊆B locally.
For the isometry assertion let Y be another Euclidean space.
Let φ:A→Y be distance preserving under L3.

argument.text: Fix a Euclidean space X, A⊆X and a real s; assume L1: s>0. Give X its Borel measurable structure. M001 with d=s identifies native μH[s](A) with the scale-cover formula. For positive s the empty-member summands vanish and each nonempty finite-diameter member has the ordinary real diameter power used in H. The supremum over extended positive scales equals the supremum over finite positive scales: the infimum at scale ∞ is no larger than the infimum at any finite scale. Countable covers are equivalent to sequences by enumeration and empty padding, with the same cost. Thus μH[s](A)=H^s(A). Restricting covers to smaller diameter bounds can only increase their infimum, so H^s_δ(A)≥H^s_r(A) whenever 0<δ≤r. The definition of H is its supremum over these contents; if that supremum is ∞, for every finite bound there is a scale exceeding the bound, and every smaller scale still exceeds it. Discharge L1 and universally generalize the arbitrary space, subset and exponent; F001 records this general statement with fresh bound names.

produces.statement: For every Euclidean space X0, subset A0⊆X0 and real p0>0, μH[p0](A0)=H^{p0}(A0); for every 0<d0≤r0, H^{p0}_{d0}(A0)≥H^{p0}_{r0}(A0). Also H^{p0}(A0)=sup_{d0>0}H^{p0}_{d0}(A0), and H^{p0}(A0)=∞ implies these contents are unbounded as the positive scale tends to zero.

argument.text: For the arbitrary X,A,s assume L6: s>0. Under the additional antecedent L7: s<dim_H(A), apply M002 with the nonnegative real u=s; F001 converts its conclusion to H^s(A)=∞, and discharging L7 proves that implication. Under L8: dim_H(A)<s, M003 similarly gives H^s(A)=0; discharge L8. Under L9: H^s(A)=0, F001 gives μH[s](A)=0≠∞, so M004 gives dim_H(A)≤s; discharge L9. Under L10: H^s(A)=∞, F001 and M005 give s≤dim_H(A); discharge L10. Discharge L6 and universally quantify the arbitrary space, subset and exponent. Nonnegativity of dimension follows from its definition as a supremum in [0,∞].

produces.statement: For every Euclidean space X0, A0⊆X0 and real p0>0: p0>dim_H(A0)⇒H^{p0}(A0)=0; p0<dim_H(A0)⇒H^{p0}(A0)=∞; H^{p0}(A0)=0⇒dim_H(A0)≤p0; H^{p0}(A0)=∞⇒dim_H(A0)≥p0. Also dim_H(A0)≥0 for every A0.

argument.text: For monotonicity fix B⊆X and temporarily assume L2: A⊆B. At every positive exponent s, any scale cover of B covers A, so its infimum bounds the content of A; taking suprema gives H^s(A)≤H^s(B). If dim_H(A)>dim_H(B), real order density supplies a finite positive exponent strictly between them (also when dim_H(A)=∞). F002 at that exponent and each set would give infinity on A and zero on B, contradicting the measure inequality. Hence dim_H(A)≤dim_H(B); discharge L2. For isometry let Y be Euclidean and assume L3: φ:A→Y preserves distances. Intersect the members of any cover of A with A and apply φ; they cover φ(A) with no greater diameters. Conversely inverse images in A of a cover of φ(A) cover A with no greater diameters, because φ preserves distance. Infima at each scale in both directions give equal contents at every positive exponent, and then H^s(φ(A))=H^s(A). If the dimensions differed, a positive finite exponent between them and F002 would again give zero on one side and infinity on the other. Discharge L3 and universally quantify X,A,B,Y,φ. The scale and critical assertions already hold universally by F001 and F002.

For arbitrary a>0, M012 at x=0 and q=a gives continuity of h↦h^a at zero, since 0≤a; its value is 0, so h^a→0 also through positive h. For arbitrary b<0, M013 gives h^b→∞ as h↓0. Finally the finite geometric identities Σ_{i=0}^{m-1}2^{-i-1}=1-2^{-m} and Σ_{i=0}^{m-1}2^{-i-2}=(1-2^{-m})/2 follow by telescoping the finite geometric sums. For m=0, 2^m≥m+1; the induction step follows from 2·(m+1)≥m+2 for m≥0. Thus 2^m≥m+1 for all natural m, so the remainders tend to zero by the Archimedean property, and taking suprema of the partial sums gives the two exported series values. Close the positive/negative exponent conditions as implications and quantify a,b.

locals.declaration: For the finite-content assertion fix s>0.
Choose R≥1 with E⊆[-R,R]^n from F001.
Fix a>n in the grid argument.
Fix arbitrary x∈V(n) for the squared-distance identity.
Fix arbitrary y∈V(n) for the squared-distance identity.

argument.text: H003 and the open-cover definition of compactness give boundedness: the nested open balls about the origin with positive integer radii cover V(n), hence E; a finite subcover is contained in one such ball and therefore in [-R,R]^n for some real R≥1. For arbitrary s>0 and δ>0 (L1), the open balls of radius δ/2 centered at points of E cover E. H003 gives a finite subcover. Each ball has diameter at most δ by the triangle inequality, so its s-cost is finite, and the finite sum bounds H^s_δ(E). Discharge L1 and quantify s,δ.

produces.statement: There exists a real R≥1 such that E⊆[-R,R]^n.
For every p0>0 and d0>0, H^{p0}_{d0}(E)<∞.

argument.text: Choose R from F001. If n>0 (L2), for 0<h≤1 and a>n (L3), divide each coordinate interval [-R,R] into ceil(2R/h) closed equal subintervals, each of length at most h. The resulting cubes cover E, number at most (2R+1)^n h^{-n}, and have diameters at most √n h: the sum of the n squared coordinate differences is at most n h². Thus their total a-cost is at most (2R+1)^n n^{a/2} h^{a-n}. By the positive-power limit in N001 this tends to zero as h↓0. For every fixed target scale and positive cost tolerance, take h small enough for both inequalities; H^a at each scale and then H^a(E) are zero. N001 gives D≤a for every a>n, hence D≤n by order density. Discharge L3,L2. If n=0 (L4), H002 and the empty-tuple definition of V(0) give E=V(0), a singleton. Its singleton cover has zero s-cost at every scale for every s>0; N001 gives D≤s for all s>0, hence D=0. Discharge L4. In both cases D≥0 by N001 and D≤n. Together with F002 this proves the dimension, boundedness and finite-content assertions.

Finally the concatenation map in V has inverse that deletes the last coordinate and records it separately. For arbitrary x,y∈V(n) and real t,u, the squared distance between the two concatenated tuples is Σ_{j<n}(x_j-y_j)^2+(t-u)^2, exactly the squared product distance. Taking nonnegative square roots proves isometry, and the displayed inverse proves bijectivity. Its restriction sends F exactly to the required E×[0,1] in V(n+1), with no change of norm.

locals.declaration: Choose the scale-r cover W with cost <ε/2 supplied by F001.

locals.declaration: For i∈K leave W_i fixed if its diameter is positive. If it is a singleton, let U_i be the closed ball centered at its unique point, of diameter min(r/2,(ε2^{-i-3})^{1/q}); n≥1 ensures that ball has exactly this positive diameter.

argument.text: Assume L1: n≥1, q>D, 0<r≤1 and ε>0, with q,r,ε arbitrary. N002 gives D≥0, hence q>0. N001 gives H^q(E)=0 and therefore H^q_r(E)=0. By the defining infimum of H^q_r, there is a countable scale-r cover of E of q-cost <ε/2: if all admissible costs were at least ε/2 their infimum would be at least ε/2. Countable covers may be enumerated by ℕ and padded with empty members.

produces.statement: There exists W:ℕ→Set V(n) covering E with diam(W_i)≤r for every i and Σ_i diam(W_i)^q<ε/2, where empty-member cost is zero; moreover q>0.

argument.text: Choose W from F001. Discard empty members and let K={i:W_i≠∅}. A nonempty zero-diameter W_i is a singleton, since distance zero identifies any two of its points. For each such i take the positive number min(r/2,(ε2^{-i-3})^{1/q}) and replace W_i by the closed ball centered at its unique point, with radius half that number. It has positive diameter at most r and q-cost ≤ε2^{-i-3}<ε2^{-i-2}; the power identity is valid because q>0. The diameter is exactly the prescribed number because n≥1: two opposite points in the first-coordinate direction belong to the closed ball, and the triangle inequality supplies the reverse diameter bound. Leave every positive-diameter member unchanged. Define U_i to be this resulting family on K and r_i=diam(U_i). The cover still contains every W_i and hence covers E, with 0<r_i≤r. Its total q-cost is at most the original cost plus Σ_{i≥0}ε2^{-i-2}≤ original cost+ε/2<ε, using the geometric sum in N001 and finite-partial-sum comparisons. This is the supplied replacement argument with an explicit permissible choice of the small diameters. Discharge L1 and universally quantify q,r,ε.

locals.declaration: In the n=0 branch fix a>1.
Fix ε>0 under L4, independently of q and δ, and later universally quantify it.
Choose K and its cover U from N003 at q,r,ε.
Choose together with K the cover U_i and write r_i=diam(U_i).
For i∈K put r_i=diam(U_i); N003 gives 0<r_i≤r.

argument.text: If n=0 (L1), N002 says that E is the singleton V(0) and D=0. For each positive integer m, divide I into m equal closed pieces and take their products with E. They cover F, each has Euclidean diameter 1/m, and their total a-cost for any a>1 is m^{1-a}=(1/m)^{a-1}→0 by N001. Diameters also tend to zero, so at each target scale the content is zero; hence H^a(F)=0. N001 gives dim_H(F)≤a for all a>1, whence dim_H(F)≤1=D+1. Discharge L1.

Now assume L2: n≥1. Fix q>D and δ>0 (L3), and independently fix ε>0 (L4). Set r=min(1,δ/√2). By N002, q>0; N003 supplies a countable cover U on K with r_i=diam(U_i)∈(0,r] and Σ_i r_i^q<ε. Set N_i=ceil(1/r_i). Partition I into N_i closed intervals [j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0≤j<N_i, of lengths 1/N_i≤r_i. Since r_i≤1, N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The products U_i×[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i] cover F and form a countable family indexed by the countable union of finite index sets. For two points in one such product, the squared distance is at most r_i²+r_i²; hence its diameter is at most √2 r_i≤δ. Their total (q+1)-cost is bounded by Σ_i N_i(√2 r_i)^{q+1}≤2(√2)^{q+1}Σ_i r_i^q<2(√2)^{q+1}ε. All diameters and costs here are finite, and q+1>0.

produces.statement: Under n≥1, q>D and δ,ε>0, H^{q+1}_δ(F)≤2(√2)^{q+1}ε.

argument.text: Discharge L4 and universally quantify ε in F002. For the fixed q and δ the content is bounded by 2(√2)^{q+1}ε for every ε>0, so the nonnegative content H^{q+1}_δ(F) is zero. This is true for every δ>0, hence H^{q+1}(F)=0. N001 gives dim_H(F)≤q+1. N002 makes D finite, and this inequality for every q>D implies dim_H(F)≤D+1: a strictly larger dimension would admit a finite q>D with q+1 below it. Discharge L3 and L2. The natural-number cases n=0 and n≥1 are exhaustive; combining with F001 gives the asserted upper bound.

locals.declaration: Fix finite ρ≥0 with diam(B)≤ρ under L1.
After proving B bounded and nonempty, define α=inf B.
After proving B bounded and nonempty, define β=sup B.

argument.text: The closed interval I=[0,1] is Borel measurable. M010 with a=0,b=1 gives λ(I)=max(1-0,0)=1.

produces.statement: I is Borel measurable and λ(I)=1.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary B,ρ,η and assume L1: B≠∅, 0≤ρ<∞, diam(B)≤ρ and η>0. For any point of B all other points lie within ρ of it, so B is bounded above and below. Real completeness gives finite α=inf B and β=sup B, with α≤b≤β for every b∈B. For every b∈B the diameter bound implies every element of B is ≤b+ρ; thus β≤b+ρ. Consequently β-ρ is a lower bound of B, so β-ρ≤α and β-α≤ρ. Define J=(α-η/2,β+η/2). Positivity of η and α≤b≤β put B inside J; its length is β-α+η>0 and ≤ρ+η. An open interval and its intersection with the closed interval I are Borel measurable. M009 with endpoints α-η/2 and β+η/2 gives λ(J)=β-α+η. Measure monotonicity gives λ(J∩I)≤λ(J)≤ρ+η. Discharge L1 and quantify B,ρ,η. Together with F001 this proves every clause of the exported enclosure statement.

argument.text: Fix s,δ and assume L1: s>0,δ>0. Put c=H^s_δ(E), finite by N002. Let W be an arbitrary scale-δ cover of F (L2), indexed by ℕ with empty padding allowed. Put ρ_i=diam(W_i)≤δ and let A_i,B_i be its two coordinate projections. The squared Euclidean product-distance formula shows each projection decreases distance. Taking suprema of distances gives diam(A_i)≤ρ_i and diam(B_i)≤ρ_i. Empty members have empty projections and zero diameter; nonempty members have nonempty projections.

produces.statement: c=H^s_δ(E)<∞; for every i, 0≤ρ_i≤δ, diam(A_i)≤ρ_i and diam(B_i)≤ρ_i; W covers F. Nonempty W_i have nonempty B_i.

argument.text: Fix ε>0 (L3) and define η_i=ε2^{-i-1}/(1+ρ_i^s)>0. For each nonempty W_i, apply N005 to B_i, the diameter bound ρ_i from F001 and η_i: define its explicit enclosing open interval J_i, of length and Lebesgue measure at most ρ_i+η_i. For empty W_i let J_i=∅. In all cases J_i and J_i∩I are Borel, B_i⊆J_i, and λ(J_i∩I)≤ρ_i+η_i. For each t∈I the A_i with t∈J_i cover E: given x∈E, (x,t)∈F lies in some W_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. By the content infimum and diam(A_i)≤ρ_i, c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). This argument makes no measurability assertion about W_i,A_i or B_i.

produces.statement: Every J_i∩I is Borel measurable, λ(J_i∩I)≤ρ_i+η_i, and for all t∈I, c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t). Here η_i=ε2^{-i-1}/(1+ρ_i^s)>0.

argument.text: Define f_i=ind(J_i∩I,ρ_i^s) on ℝ. Each is measurable: on the Borel set J_i∩I it is a constant and on its Borel complement it is zero; inverse images of Borel sets are therefore one of these sets, ∅, or ℝ. In particular it is λ-almost-everywhere measurable. F002 gives ind(I,c)≤Σ_i f_i pointwise on all ℝ, since outside I both sides vanish.

produces.statement: Every f_i=ind(J_i∩I,ρ_i^s) is measurable and hence λ-almost-everywhere measurable; on all ℝ, ind(I,c)≤Σ_i f_i pointwise.

argument.text: M008 applied to the pointwise inequality F003 gives the corresponding inequality of nonnegative integrals. M007 on I with c and N005's λ(I)=1 identifies the left integral with c. M006 exchanges the nonnegative sum and integral, using the measurability already proved in F003; M007 on each J_i∩I with coefficient ρ_i^s then gives c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s λ(J_i∩I). By F002 this is at most Σ_i ρ_i^{s+1}+Σ_i η_iρ_i^s≤Σ_i ρ_i^{s+1}+ε, since η_iρ_i^s=ε2^{-i-1}ρ_i^s/(1+ρ_i^s)≤ε2^{-i-1} and N001 gives Σ_i2^{-i-1}=1. The product and sum comparisons follow first for finite partial sums and then by their suprema; thus they remain valid if a series is infinite. This is Tonelli for nonnegative terms, without finite-integrability premises or an exchange of signed series.

produces.statement: For the arbitrary ε>0 and cover W, c≤Σ_i ρ_i^{s+1}+ε.

argument.text: Discharge L3 and quantify ε in F004: for every ε>0, c≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1}+ε. If the series is infinite, c≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1} is immediate. Otherwise it is a finite real, and order density applied to the inequality for every ε>0 gives c≤Σ_iρ_i^{s+1}. Since W was an arbitrary δ-cover, c is a lower bound of every admissible (s+1)-cost; therefore c≤H^{s+1}_δ(F), their infimum. Discharge L2, then L1, and universally quantify s,δ. This proves the asserted inequality with exactly the same scale on both sides.

argument.text: Assume L1: D>0. N002 gives finite D. Fix 0<s<D (L2). By N001, H^s(E)=∞, so H^s_δ(E) is unbounded as δ↓0. N006 gives H^s_δ(E)≤H^{s+1}_δ(F) for each δ>0. Taking suprema over δ proves H^{s+1}(F)=∞. N001 therefore gives dim_H(F)≥s+1.

Discharge L2 and quantify s: dim_H(F)≥s+1 for every 0<s<D. These s exist because D>0. Their supremum is D, by real order density. Hence dim_H(F)≥D+1. Discharge L1 to obtain exactly the exported conditional lower bound.

argument.text: For arbitrary a>1 (L1), partition I into m equal closed subintervals for every positive integer m. Diameters are 1/m and total a-cost is m^{1-a}=(1/m)^{a-1}→0 by N001. At any fixed positive target scale these covers eventually qualify and have arbitrarily small cost. Hence every scale content and H^a(I) are zero; N001 yields dim_H(I)≤a for all a>1, and thus dim_H(I)≤1. Discharge L1 and quantify a.

argument.text: Fix 0<s<1 and δ>0 (L2), and any scale-δ cover W of I (L3), with ρ_i=diam(W_i)≤δ. For arbitrary ε>0 (L4), enclose each nonempty W_i in the open interval J_i provided by N005 with η=ε2^{-i-1}; take J_i=∅ for empty W_i. These intervals cover I and satisfy λ(J_i)≤ρ_i+ε2^{-i-1}. By N005, λ(I)=1; measure monotonicity and M011 applied to J give 1≤λ(⋃_iJ_i)≤Σ_iλ(J_i)≤Σ_iρ_i+ε, the last estimate using the geometric sum in N001 and finite-partial-sum comparisons. Let ε↓0: if Σ_iρ_i is infinite the conclusion is automatic, otherwise order density gives Σ_iρ_i≥1. Discharge L4. Arbitrary covering sets need not be measurable, since only the enclosing intervals have entered the length estimate.

produces.statement: For the arbitrary scale-δ cover W of I, Σ_iρ_i≥1, where ρ_i=diam(W_i)≤δ.

argument.text: For positive ρ_i≤δ and s<1, ρ_i^{s-1}≥δ^{s-1}, so ρ_i^s≥δ^{s-1}ρ_i. For ρ_i=0 the same inequality is 0≥0 because s>0. Summing finite partial sums and taking their suprema gives Σ_iρ_i^s≥δ^{s-1}Σ_iρ_i≥δ^{s-1} by F002. Since W was arbitrary, infimizing gives H^s_δ(I)≥δ^{s-1}. Discharge L3. N001 gives δ^{s-1}→∞ as δ↓0 because s-1<0; consequently H^s(I)=∞. N001 gives dim_H(I)≥s for every 0<s<1, so dim_H(I)≥1 by order density. Discharge L2 and quantify s,δ. With F001 this proves all clauses of the exported interval-dimension statement.

argument.text: N002 gives 0≤D≤n and finite D. If D>0 (L1), N007 gives dim_H(F)≥D+1; discharge L1. If D=0 (L2), choose x_0∈E by H002 and define φ:I→V(n)×ℝ by φ(t)=(x_0,t). The Euclidean product-distance formula gives d(φ(t),φ(u))=|t-u|, so φ is distance preserving and φ(I)⊆F. N001 gives dim_H(φ(I))=dim_H(I) and monotonicity gives dim_H(F)≥dim_H(φ(I)). N008 states dim_H(I)=1, hence dim_H(F)≥1=D+1 in this branch, including n=0. Discharge L2. Nonnegativity makes these cases exhaustive. N004 supplies the opposite bound, giving dim_H(F)=D+1. Finally N002's bijective concatenation isometry identifies this exact metric and set with E×[0,1]⊆ℝ^{n+1}; by N001 the dimension is unchanged. Substitution of D=dim_H(E) proves the full target.
